title: Boss: linear structures
summary: A calculator, a list merge, a stack that knows its minimum, and a game of hot potato.

steps.title: Reverse Polish calculator
prompt: In **postfix** notation the operator comes after its two operands: `3 4 +` means `3 + 4`, and `5 1 2 + 4 * + 3 -` means `5 + (1 + 2) * 4 - 3`. No brackets are ever needed.
Write `int EvalRpn(string expr)`. Tokens are separated by single spaces; operators are `+ - * /` (integer division).
Use a `Stack<int>`: push numbers; for an operator pop **two** numbers, apply it, push the result. Careful with the order: the first pop is the **right** operand.
```csharp
solution: stack.Push(token switch { "+" => left + right, "-" => left - right, "*" => left * right, _ => left / right });
hints: Split on spaces. A token like `-6` is a number, not an operator, so compare whole tokens.
For an operator: `int right = stack.Pop(); int left = stack.Pop();` then push `left op right`.

steps.title: Merge two sorted lists
prompt: The tests provide `class Node { public int Value; public Node? Next; public Node(int value, Node? next) }`.

Write `Node? MergeSorted(Node? a, Node? b)`: both lists are sorted ascending; return one sorted list that **reuses their nodes** (do not create new nodes except, if you like, one dummy starting node).
```text
Tip: a dummy node `var dummy = new Node(0, null); var tail = dummy;` avoids special-casing the first node. Return `dummy.Next`.
solution: if (a.Value <= b.Value) { tail.Next = a; a = a.Next; }
template: Node? DojoBuild(params int[] values) { Node? h = null; for (var i = values.Length - 1; i >= 0; i--) h = new Node(values[i], h); return h; }
string DojoShow(Node? h) { var parts = new List<string>(); for (var c = h; c != null; c = c.Next) parts.Add(c.Value.ToString()); return string.Join(",", parts); }
Dojo.Check("reuses the original nodes", ReferenceEquals(dojoMerged, dojoA), "the first node should be the 5 node from list a");
public Node(int value, Node? next) { Value = value; Next = next; }
hints: While both lists have nodes, attach the smaller head to `tail` and advance that list.
When one list runs out, attach the rest of the other: `tail.Next = a ?? b;`.

steps.title: A stack that knows its minimum
prompt: Write a class `MinStack` where **every** operation is `O(1)`:
- `void Push(int x)`
- `int Pop()`: throws `InvalidOperationException` when empty
- `int Min()`: the smallest value currently in the stack; throws `InvalidOperationException` when empty
Scanning the whole stack in `Min` would be `O(n)`. Trick: keep a **second** stack holding the minimum-so-far at every level.
template: for (var dojoI = 200_000; dojoI > 0; dojoI--) { dojoBig.Push(dojoI); dojoBig.Min(); }
for (var dojoI = 1; dojoI < 100_000; dojoI++) { dojoBig.Pop(); dojoBig.Min(); }
Dojo.Eq("300,000 mixed operations stay fast", 100_000, dojoBig.Min());
hints: On push, also push `Math.Min(x, mins.Peek())` onto `mins` (or `x` if `mins` is empty).
On pop, pop both stacks. `Min()` is `mins.Peek()`.

steps.title: Hot potato
prompt: Players `1` to `n` sit in a circle. Counting starts at player 1; every `k`-th player is eliminated, and counting carries on from the next player. Write `int LastStanding(int n, int k)`.
```text
n = 5, k = 2: eliminated 2, 4, 1, 5; player 3 wins
Model the circle with a `Queue<int>`: to pass the potato, dequeue a player and enqueue them again at the back. The `k`-th one is dequeued and **not** put back.
solution: for (var p = 1; p <= n; p++) circle.Enqueue(p);
for (var i = 1; i < k; i++) circle.Enqueue(circle.Dequeue());
template: Dojo.Eq("k = 1 removes in order: player n wins", 6, LastStanding(6, 1));
hints: Enqueue 1..n. While more than one player remains, move `k - 1` players from front to back, then dequeue one for good.
The last one left in the queue is the winner.
